The Invisible Hand

A text about who makes things happen — and who disappears from the sentence when they do.

Causative verb
Passive voice
Listen to the text
0:000:00

Every morning, before Nara opens her eyes, the algorithm has already had her feed curated. By the time she reaches for her phone, a version of the world has been assembled for her: the products she is likely to want, the opinions she is likely to find persuasive, the people whose lives will make her feel behind. She did not ask for this. She does not refuse it either.

The system does not make Nara do anything in the way that a command does. It works more quietly than that. It gets her to want things she did not know she lacked. A bag she never needed becomes, after fourteen impressions, something she feels she has been missing. Her desire has been manufactured for her so smoothly that the manufacturing is invisible.

Bernays understood this a hundred years ago. He got an entire generation to associate cigarettes with freedom. He did not lie, exactly. He simply placed the right objects in the hands of the right people and let the public believe that the desire was their own. The technique has not changed. Only the medium has.

Huxley saw the endpoint. In his World State, citizens are not forced into happiness — they have their happiness designed for them before they are born. The conditioning is so complete that the question of freedom never arises. Soma makes them feel exactly what the system needs them to feel. No one refuses. There is nothing to refuse against.

This is what Zuboff calls behavioural modification at scale. The platform does not punish the wrong choices — it makes the wrong choices seem unthinkable. It gets you to stay not through walls but through a variable reward schedule that your nervous system was never designed to resist.

Nara has never thought of herself as someone who lets the system decide what she wants. She thinks of herself as someone with taste, with preferences, with a carefully considered sense of who she is. And she is right, in a way. The preferences are real. The question is only: who had them designed?

The answer, Huxley would say, does not change the feeling. A cage that makes you love it is still a cage. It is simply a better one.

Before part two

Five questions of concept.

No correct answer. Take a position and defend it.

01
Is desire that was engineered still genuine — or does its origin change what it is?
Frankfurt argues that what makes a desire genuinely yours is not where it came from, but whether you endorse it at a higher level — through what he calls second-order desires — whether you reflectively endorse your desire — if you want to want it — then it is genuinely yours, regardless of where it originated. The problem Huxley raises: what if the capacity for reflection was itself engineered?|||–">want to want it. Huxley disagrees implicitly: if the endorsement itself was engineered, the hierarchy collapses. Both positions are defensible.
Your position
02
The text argues the system works through persuasion, not force. Does that distinction matter morally?
Bernays thought it did — he believed engineering consent was more democratic than coercion because it respected the appearance of choice. Huxley thought the distinction was the most dangerous illusion of all: a cage that persuades you to enter is harder to escape than one that traps you. Who bears more moral responsibility — the system, or the person who consents?
Your position
03
Huxley's citizens are not forced — they are designed to love what the system needs them to love. Is that a form of freedom, or its opposite?
Huxley's argument in Brave New World Revisited (1958) is explicit: the most insidious form of tyranny is the one that feels like contentment. John the Savage, the only character who rejects it, chooses suffering over engineered happiness — and Huxley treats that as the only authentically human choice available. Is John right, or is he simply attached to a different kind of conditioning?
Your position
04
If resistance always gets absorbed by the system — turned into a brand, a lifestyle, a market — does that mean resistance is pointless?
Mark Fisher called this the defining feature of capitalist realism: the system is "a monstrous, infinitely plastic entity, capable of metabolizing and absorbing anything with which it comes into contact." Punk becomes a clothing line. Environmentalism becomes a product category. But Fisher did not conclude that resistance was pointless — only that resistance must operate at the level of imagination, not lifestyle. What would that look like?
Your position
05
Is it possible to want something that the system did not, in some way, put there first?
Bernays believed it was not — that all desire is a displaced symbol of something the culture makes available. Frankfurt's framework suggests a possible exit: if you can reflect on a desire and genuinely endorse it as your own, the causal origin becomes less relevant. Huxley's counter: reflection itself is a product of the culture that shaped you. The question may be unanswerable — which is precisely why it is worth asking.
